subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Buffers maintain pH by balancing weak acids and bases, crucial for enzyme activity and cellular function. Clinicians use buffer status to assess metabolic and respiratory disorders.

sections.p: Buffers are systems of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid) that resist pH change when acids or bases are added.
The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation relates pH to the ratio of conjugate base to acid. Small changes in H⁺ are absorbed by the buffer components.

t.b: Determines pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻ to identify respiratory vs metabolic disturbances; abnormal values indicate inadequate buffering.

sections.p: Homeostatic organs (lungs, kidneys, blood proteins) adjust buffer components. Respiratory compensation changes CO₂; renal compensation adjusts bicarbonate.
Impaired buffering leads to acid–base disorders. Causes include renal failure, severe diarrhea, sepsis, or toxin ingestion.
b: Metabolic acidosis: low HCO₃⁻, high anion gap; respiratory alkalosis: low PaCO₂

sections.p: Buffer status guides treatment: bicarbonate therapy, ventilation adjustments, or dialysis. Recognizing buffer failure prevents organ damage.
b: Severe acidosis can depress myocardial contractility and cause arrhythmias

t.b: Low indicates metabolic acidosis; high suggests metabolic alkalosis.
High suggests respiratory acidosis; low indicates respiratory alkalosis.

sections.p: Remember the three main buffer systems: bicarbonate, phosphate, hemoglobin. Use Henderson–Hasselbalch to calculate expected pH changes.
b: Bicarbonate buffer dominates in plasma; phosphate in intracellular fluids; hemoglobin in red cells.

faq.q: What is the most important buffer in blood?
faq.a: The bicarbonate–CO₂ system, because it accounts for ~70% of plasma buffering capacity.

faq.q: How does hemoglobin act as a buffer?
faq.a: Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds H⁺ released from CO₂ hydration, reducing pH change during tissue oxygen extraction (Haldane effect).
Yes, high intake of acidic foods can lower plasma bicarbonate, but the body compensates via renal excretion and respiratory adjustments.

exam: Explain how the bicarbonate buffer system compensates for a sudden drop in blood pH.
Describe the laboratory findings in a patient with chronic renal failure leading to metabolic acidosis.
Differentiate between respiratory and metabolic causes of a low arterial pH using blood gas values.
